title: 2026-2910: technical construction and mechanism reasoning
body:
# 2026-2910: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## Original BLITZ: two mirrored four-bar collectors

Version: BLITZ original. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=5) · [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=8)

**Published construction:** Dual four-bars; X44 deployment at 79.37:1; separate X60 roller drives.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Collect sideways while passing; collapse under impacts.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** This is a coupled routing decision. Collecting on either side allows the chassis to translate across a fuel pile while its fixed shooter points toward the destination. That can recover some of the directional independence normally purchased with a turret. A four-bar can also move backward under a frontal impact, but only if the linkage, motor controller, chain and hard stops permit that motion. More joints create more wear locations, and both collectors consume the space that another architecture could use for a hopper. The second intake should therefore be evaluated by additional useful fuel delivered, rather than the visual symmetry of the mechanism.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare opposite-side sweep paths against turning a single-intake robot, including one damaged linkage and time to replace it.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Original BLITZ: serpentine inventory and passing

Version: BLITZ original. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=5) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Serpentine conveyor, two X60 feeder motors, three X60 shooter motors; variable hood.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Use the alliance zone as storage for a passing-centered role.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The low-storage concept treats the field as an external buffer. Its success requires the alliance to recover that buffered fuel at the right time and place. Passing capacity and scoring capacity are different services even when the same launcher performs both. A continuous serpentine can constrain fuel well but adds contact length, curved transitions and friction; a well-controlled ball path may still be unable to supply enough mass flow. This original brief must be read alongside the later rebuild account: a design rationale is evidence of a hypothesis, not evidence that the hypothesis met the team’s competitive targets.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure fuel moved to a recoverable location, residual path inventory, and scoring available after the passer returns; vary partner collection quality.

**Limits:** The brief describes a 25-fuel/s feed capability; the later account reports inadequate overall performance. Do not treat that number as an independently demonstrated match average.

## RE-BLITZ: strengthened slapdown

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Four-bar replaced by slapdown; 0.6-inch plates; #35 deployment chain; powered bottom roller.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Strength, service access and reliable full-speed acquisition.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A single pivot simplifies the force path: an exposed roller loads its arms, pivot and hard stop without several moving links sharing the impact. That does not make it automatically more impact tolerant. The stronger arm and larger deployment chain need a corresponding chassis attachment and a stop that can react a collision without loading the gearbox teeth. Powering the lower contact also matters at the bumper transition: fuel can otherwise be caught between a moving upper roller and a stationary surface while the robot continues advancing. Plate stiffness and ball transport are separate improvements and should be tested separately.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test a wall hit and an oblique corner hit, then remeasure roller alignment and deployment current; test full-speed pickup of worn fuel.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: preserve width through the floor and tower

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10)

**Published construction:** Ten inclined floor rollers; four-X60 feeder; Teflon backing; enlarged four-wide path.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Remove restrictions between hopper and launcher.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Adding a fourth release lane helps only if four lanes remain supplied. A floor feeding a narrow or irregular throat produces alternating bursts and starvation even when the drum has ample power. Inclination and backing determine the normal force and the direction in which fuel escapes when multiple balls arrive together. Low-friction backing reduces the energy lost to sliding while powered rollers maintain forward contact. An open path also needs a controlled final approach: a ball entering the launch contact at a variable velocity or height changes compression and the exit state. Diagnose the last few balls separately from the first dense volley.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Log feeder current, wheel speed and scored output through a full hopper; repeat with 5, 15 and 30 fuel and with deliberate asymmetric loading.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: drum, hood rollers and flywheel recovery

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10)

**Published construction:** Four-inch drum, 1.5-inch hood rollers, overdriven flywheel; team reports >30 fuel/s and a 34 maximum.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** High discharge rate with manageable shooter recovery.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A drum’s useful contact surface is a distributed launch interface. If fuel encounters different compression along its width, the nominally identical lanes can launch at different speeds. Flywheel energy can cover short impulses while the motors replace average energy, but a dense volley still requires sufficient sustained electrical power. Surface condition, ball wear and hood contact determine how much of the wheel’s speed becomes translation versus spin. The reported rate is valuable as a team result; it does not establish accuracy, defended performance, battery condition or an all-match average. Copy the geometry only with a plan to characterize those conditions.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure per-lane velocity and accuracy before and after a long volley; log loaded battery voltage and recovery between successive shots.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: expansion actuated by the intake

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p11](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=11)

**Published construction:** Intake-driven hopper expansion; smooth internal sheet-metal joints; deployed one-way catchers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Store useful inventory and feed it back toward the shooter.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The expanding walls and intake form one mechanism state machine. A wall that expands independently without managing its overlap can create a ledge, trap fuel, or fight the intake during retraction. Smooth fasteners reduce snagging, while the deployed catches react loads that should not be carried continuously by the intake motor. A large hopper helps separate acquisition from discharge, giving the driver freedom to reposition. That freedom disappears if the final fuel cannot leave without a specific intake movement. The recommendation should therefore specify both the retained capacity and the emptying sequence.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Interrupt deployment halfway with a full hopper; test reverse motion, ball trapping at panel overlaps, trench travel and final-fuel evacuation.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: mechanism readiness and fallback operation

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p12](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=13)

**Published construction:** Shot gates, vision-based targeting, CANrange preload sensing and fixed-position manual fallbacks.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Coordinate feeding with the actual launch state.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A high mechanical ceiling can be lost to premature feed. The feeder must distinguish an intentional firing pause from a jam, an empty hopper and a shooter that has not recovered. Readiness should use measured values with hysteresis rather than one noisy threshold. Manual known-position shots preserve a useful degraded mode when localization fails, but require practiced driver cues and a stable mechanical zero. A mechanism database needs this control contract because an intake, indexer and drum borrowed from different robots may otherwise disagree about who owns the next ball.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Disable one camera, introduce an empty-hopper sensor error and force a heading correction mid-volley; check the operator can recover predictably.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Drive | Mk5n R2; X60 drive; X44 steer | [Source p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=7) |
| Intake | 79.37:1 deploy; mirrored four-bars | [Source p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=8) |
| Shooter | three X60 launch motors; one X44 hood | [Source p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=9) |
| Drive | 27.5×27-in frame; Mk5n R1 | [Source p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=8) |
| Intake | 40:1 deploy; #35 chain; 2-in and 1.25-in rollers | [Source p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=9) |
| Floor | 15° inclination; ten 1.25-in rollers; four-X60 feeder | [Source p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10) |
| Shooter | 4-in drum; 1.5-in hood rollers; 6.7:1 flywheel overdrive source description | [Source p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10) |

title: 2026-3467: technical construction and mechanism reasoning
body:
# 2026-3467: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## 3467: redundant rack support and expanding walls

Version: 2026 dual shooter. [PDF p9](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=9) · [PDF p10](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=10)

**Published construction:** Double polycarbonate rack plates; powered and idler pinions; walls move with intake.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Impact tolerance, tooth engagement and more storage.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Supporting a rack at more than one point reduces its tendency to peel away from the drive pinion under load. Two rack plates can distribute stress, but only if their tooth timing and guidance are aligned; otherwise they can fight each other. Moving the walls with the collector creates agitation as well as extra volume. Agitation may improve flow near the floor but can also throw a top layer out unless the lid and wall overlap control it. A side load remains a separate case from a frontal collapse.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test rack deflection, skipping and skew with a side hit; observe fuel near moving wall seams during repeated deploy/retract cycles.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 3467: active centering into two launch streams

Version: 2026 dual shooter. [PDF p11](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=11) · [PDF p12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=12)

**Published construction:** Ten floor rollers; powered stacked-belt side wedges; central divider; live-axle tower roller.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Center fuel while limiting tower oscillation.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Active side contact can rotate or translate fuel away from a bottleneck rather than relying on gravity against a fixed wall. Its surface direction has to agree with the desired stream; excessive inward force can create an arch at the divider. The live-axle tower roller is a structural answer to rapidly changing multi-ball loads, reducing a source of compression variation. The useful comparison is not simply belts versus rollers: it is whether the particular contact geometry establishes two repeatable, supplied paths through the entire range of hopper fill.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Feed off-center piles, log each stream separately, and compare tower deflection under single-ball and paired-ball arrivals.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 3467: two independent launchers and stored energy

Version: 2026 dual shooter. [PDF p13](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=13) · [PDF p14](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=14)

**Published construction:** Two launchers; four 3-inch 45A wheels per launcher with inertia kits; adjustable hood.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** High rate with controllable exit conditions.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Independent launch drives can compensate for asymmetric supply, but increase the number of conditions that must be measured. Added inertia can reduce transient speed droop while consuming mass and spin-up time. A soft wheel increases compliance and contact duration, but changes compression as it wears or heats. Hood range should be translated into a validated scoring and passing envelope, rather than assuming every geometric angle produces a useful trajectory. The desired test is a full stream of representative fuel, not a single ideal ball launched repeatedly.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare both streams’ exit speed distributions and accuracy through a long volley, at fresh and worn surface conditions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 3467: camera structure and predictive trench ducking

Version: 2026 dual shooter. [PDF p15](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=15) · [PDF p19](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=19) · [PDF p20](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=20)

**Published construction:** Braced camera towers; measured shot gates; future-pose hood retraction for trench entry.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Preserve localization and avoid hood collisions.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Camera vibration produces an apparent pose error even if the vision algorithm is otherwise correct. Bracing the mount to the shooter can stiffen it, but also transmits shooter vibration; the net effect should be measured. Trench protection is a dynamic clearance problem: retracting at the boundary is too late when the mechanism takes time to move. The lookahead should include speed, control delay, deceleration and an uncertainty margin, with a safe fallback if localization becomes invalid. This is a control requirement created by the mechanism’s envelope.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Run approach tests at several speeds and headings with degraded pose data; verify the hood clears before the physical entry plane.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

# 2026-4414: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## RIPCURRENT: shape the chassis and bumpers around the feed system

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Chamfered 25×32-inch base; offset battery rail; structural bumper/hopper walls and low electronics.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Preserve low rotor diameter and storage area within the perimeter.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A singulator occupies a swept area, not just a rectangular bounding box. Changing chassis corners can preserve the parts of that area that most improve ring diameter while removing less useful perimeter. Moving the battery to an edge creates a new structural problem because the rail still has to carry drive and impact loads. Using the bumper backing as a hopper boundary can reclaim interior width, while tying scorer alignment to a removable impact structure. The package needs a repeatable bumper interface, and the stored-fuel center of mass must be evaluated alongside the empty robot.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Reinstall bumpers and measure scorer alignment; test loaded lateral acceleration and rotor clearance after representative impacts.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: independently driven rotor, packing relief and passive contact

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Separate rotor/feed drives; shaped fin and wrap guides; passive rollers and omni contacts.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce packing pressure, friction and belt slip.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A bulk pile can load the singulator even when the exit path is clear. Agitating the pile and supplying the launch stream are different motions, so separating drives gives useful tuning freedom. A shaped fin can alter where that pile pressure is released; passive rollers reduce sliding resistance where balls push against each other. These details explain why a DYE-inspired design cannot be generalized as a generic circular indexer. The critical behavior is the changing network of contacts at full, partial and nearly empty loads, including a controlled reverse to clear a bridge.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure stream continuity and current at several load states; observe whether agitation increases entry occupancy or merely recirculates fuel.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: compliant racks and a separately latched lower contact

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Stacked polycarbonate racks; primary and lower powered rollers; strengthened hubs and shear interfaces.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Impact compliance and reliable pickup with retained storage.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Stacking plates can create controlled flex only if the plates and fasteners permit the intended relative motion. A low roller that remains deployed adds another ownership contact near the bumper, while its latch removes continuous holding load from an actuator. Stronger hubs and distributed shear interfaces address local failure modes that a thicker arm alone may not fix. The collector also moves storage boundaries, so its success must be measured while the hopper is loaded and the side walls are being pushed by fuel.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test diagonal wall contact, rack synchronization and lower-latch retention; inspect roller-end alignment and capacity after impact.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: compact shooter swept volume and stored energy

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Four-X44 3-inch flywheel; added dense inertia; powered hood roller; vertically stacked motor package.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce protrusions while preserving the desired launch contact.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A compact turret can improve the whole robot by leaving more feed and storage volume around its swept envelope. That benefit must be weighed against launch-contact repeatability, motor cooling, wire access and flywheel recovery. Dense inertia stores energy in limited space, but increases spin-up energy and bearing loads. A powered hood contact changes the spin state and must remain geometrically consistent as the hood moves. The key comparison with a drum is delivered scored fuel during usable windows, including time moving and acquiring, rather than a single instantaneous output rate.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map exit velocity and spin versus hood angle, turret heading and volley length; inspect belt tracking under acceleration.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: calibration and uncertainty remain empirical

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/116)

**Published construction:** Team reply describes robust-shot selection followed by measured angle and velocity calibration.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Choose trajectories tolerant of exit-state errors.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A nominal ballistic solution is not enough when fuel compression, wear and launch contact change the actual exit velocity. Searching for a region of successful trajectories can improve tolerance, but the model must be anchored to measurements of the real mechanism. Separate localization, hood-reference and exit-speed errors before retuning: otherwise one correction can conceal another. This is a transferable technical procedure, not evidence that every team should adopt the same equation set or that the robot can score under every motion and defense condition.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Use stationary known-pose tests to isolate launch error, then add translation, rotation and tilt one at a time.

**Limits:** Construction is from the previously reviewed binder and current indexed binder text; calibration explanation is from team reply /519602/116. Current direct binder download returned 403. Existing source images were retained; no new visual watching is claimed.

# 2026-6800: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## DOWNPOUR original: linear collection and linked hopper

Version: DOWNPOUR original turret. [PDF p11](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=11) · [PDF p12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=12)

**Published construction:** Rack deployment, multiple powered rollers, pin-slot hopper extension.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Compact stow and broad acquisition.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The intake and expanding wall are physically linked, so their travel, friction and alignment cannot be optimized independently. A pin-slot joint can accommodate different trajectories but may create a high local pressure at the end of travel. A multirotor pickup needs enough overlap to avoid an uncontrolled interval as fuel crosses the bumper. If the linkage binds, commanding more motor torque can damage the rack before solving the wall alignment. The architecture should retain a way to inspect and replace the joint without disassembling the whole fuel path.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Cycle the linkage under hopper side loading and inspect slot wear; test an interrupted deployment and recovery.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR original: serpentine and turret feed

Version: DOWNPOUR original turret. [PDF p13](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=13) · [PDF p14](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=14) · [PDF p15](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=15)

**Published construction:** Belt serpentine; curved backing replaces interfering upper wheels; 400° turret.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Compact routing with controlled feed and independent aim.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Removing a wheel can improve a mechanism when the wheel occupies the same space needed by another moving assembly. Curved backing trades active contact for sliding contact and must keep fuel captured through the bend. The turret’s rotation range is a cable-management specification as much as an aiming specification. The original design and its later replacement are separate records: a successful collection system does not prove the single-stream scorer met the team’s later competitive needs. Prototype targets must remain labeled targets even when the surrounding prose sounds confident.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Sweep the full turret range while feeding deliberately varied fuel, and compare useful output with the original target under realistic voltage.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR DCMP: repair the collision path

Version: DOWNPOUR DCMP drum. [PDF p4](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=4)

**Published construction:** Single-pivot intake; higher round bash bar; extra motor-plate bracing; passive lower bar.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Stop bar deflection from stalling rollers; save power and weight.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A bash bar can become the failure if it bends into the very roller it protects. Moving the reaction member above the rotating contact changes that failure geometry. Reverting a powered element to a passive surface is an important counterexample to the rule that more powered contacts always help: the added drive may cost current without improving capture in the tested geometry. This result should not be transferred blindly to another bumper gap or approach speed. It supports testing the actual bottleneck and force path before adding a motor.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure bar-to-roller clearance after impact; compare capture probability and current with powered and passive lower contact.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR DCMP: net, trench access and electrical relocation

Version: DOWNPOUR DCMP drum. [PDF p3](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=3) · [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=5)

**Published construction:** Net-topped storage; bumper-mounted panels; electrical panel flipped upward.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Retain fuel, use trench routes and protect electronics.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A bumper-mounted wall can simplify robot mass allocation but introduces a service interface: removing or shifting the bumper can change hopper alignment and expose a gap. The net adds a travel envelope that depends on fuel loading and deformation. Flipping the electrical panel exchanges one exposure for another, so the skid plate, drainage and access plan must be considered with the new layout. The correct capacity test measures fuel retained after the actual route and then delivered to the shooter, rather than the empty CAD volume.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Remove and reinstall bumpers repeatedly, inspect wall alignment, then run full-load trench and bump routes followed by complete discharge.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR DCMP: single-stream turret to four-wide drum

Version: DOWNPOUR DCMP drum. [PDF p2](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=2) · [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=6) · [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=7)

**Published construction:** Four-wide transfer; mixed-diameter rollers; three X60 shooter drives and two feeder drives.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Original single stream was too slow for the intended competition level.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The rebuild changes both the launcher and the supply path. Wider discharge without wider feeding would preserve the original restriction. Gradually accelerating fuel can reduce crowding before launch, but it must preserve contact and avoid forcing balls against a stationary roof. The strategic claim is specific to this team’s execution and operating conditions; it does not invalidate compact turrets that achieve a different combination of capacity, sustained firing and maneuverability. Preserve the original development and the district-to-DCMP transition so a recommendation can learn from the pivot rather than only its final appearance.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare complete cycle score against the original under the same fuel supply, defense and active-window timing.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR: proposed telescope and later compact hooks

Version: DOWNPOUR DCMP drum. [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=8)

**Published construction:** Original telescope did not compete at districts; later pivoting hooks replaced it.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Weight, space and scoring priorities displaced the initial climb.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The presence of a climber CAD image in an early binder is not proof it was installed or used. The later brief supplies a useful version boundary by explicitly saying the earlier mechanism did not compete. The new hook package should be recorded as a compact capability, not evidence that climbing became strategically central. In a fuel-dominant game, retain the opportunity cost in storage, mechanism power, alignment and testing. A low-mass hook can still be a poor choice if it blocks a valuable fuel route.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Audit actual installation and match use separately from prototype drawings; calculate lost usable fuel volume before selecting a climbing package.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

# 2026-9470: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## 9470: triple-channel scorer to an open drum path

Version: 9470 engineering reference and version history. [Technical source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/)

**Published construction:** Triple shooter at early events; DCMP drum uses a full-width roller, pivoting hood rollers and three feeder rollers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Higher ceiling without a channel-settling step.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The significant change is the removal of restrictive channel interfaces, not simply a larger launch wheel. Dividers can stabilize a piece path while creating an arch or an extra alignment delay; an open drum path can accept a broader front but needs consistent compression across its width. The early triple shooter remains an intentional schedule choice rather than a failed idea in every context. A team with an early event can rationally choose a lower ceiling that preserves practice time, then rebuild once the feed and current demands are understood.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare first-shot delay, sustained output and nearly-empty-hopper output across both configurations under the same supply conditions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 9470: reinforce the proven failure while preserving geometry

Version: 9470 engineering reference and version history. [Technical source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/)

**Published construction:** Worlds intake uses stacked quarter-inch SRP side plates with leaf-spring mounting and reinforced motor plates.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** DCMP damage made intake survival the next priority.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Changing material without changing the mounting boundary may fail to create the intended compliance. A leaf-spring arrangement needs room to bend, a predictable load path and fasteners that do not clamp the compliant region into an unintended rigid joint. Reinforcing the motor plate addresses a concentrated load while preserving the pickup geometry that the drivers already know. This is a useful rebuild principle: once the collection and shot behavior work, the largest improvement may be a structural interface that prevents losing the entire match rather than another nominal-rate optimization.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure deflection and residual alignment after repeatable corner hits, and time a side-plate replacement without disturbing the roller assembly.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 9470: floor redesign follows the scorer and service needs

Version: 9470 engineering reference and version history. [Technical source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/)

**Published construction:** Final floor has eight mixed-compliance rollers, one X60 and a two-screw pivot for access.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Simpler feeding and fast electronics service.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A floor that works for one shooter architecture may create unnecessary volume and transfer stages for another. Mixing hard tubes and compliant contacts can maintain support while encouraging fuel through a problematic region. The service pivot adds a deliberate state outside gameplay: technicians must be able to open the floor, reach electronics and restore alignment quickly. That can improve event reliability more than reducing a small amount of mass. Include cable routing, fastener retention and the post-service check in the architecture record.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Time an actual electrical repair through the pivot, then verify floor alignment and feeding after repeated open/close cycles.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 9470: empirical calibration and practice deadline

Version: 9470 engineering reference and version history. [Technical source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/)

**Published construction:** Interpolated shot map, measured first-shot correction and time-of-flight lookahead; fixed pre-event ship deadline.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Preserve practice and tuning time.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** An empirical map can be a technically rigorous choice when it captures the dominant real-world exit behavior within the available build window. It still needs enough sampling, a stable mechanical reference and a policy for replacing worn surfaces or changing fuel. The deadline is part of the architecture’s feasibility: every additional mechanism competes with the time needed to calibrate and drive it. A borrowed model should include its data-collection procedure and failure fallback rather than promising accuracy from a published algorithm name.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Repeat calibration after surface replacement and at low battery, then validate moving shots outside the original tuning trajectories.

**Limits:** The process page is a team account. Dynamic homepage counters rendered as zero in static retrieval and were not imported as historical records; one L1 valuation on the page is not accepted as a rules authority.

title: Technical evidence, load paths, contact mechanics and validation
body:
# Reading technical evidence as an architecture agent

The mechanism notes separate five layers: published construction, the team's stated reason, original engineering interpretation, a proposed validation test, and remaining limits. The analysis is not an undisclosed quote from the team. A detailed explanation of why a contact or load path can work is not proof that the team measured that effect. When the source merely lists specifications, the stated-reason field explicitly says so. Do not convert a plausible mechanical explanation into a historical claim about the team's intent.

## A useful technical description follows the piece and the load

For an intake, identify the first powered contact, the supporting surface, the point where ownership becomes secure and every transition before storage. State the acquisition envelope and the failure when the piece arrives diagonally, at a wall, in a pile or at maximum approach speed. A wide mouth can have a narrow effective capture area if its outer contacts eject rather than center. A motor count does not reveal whether a dead zone interrupts ownership. Record material, wheel geometry, compression, power transmission, deployment kinematics and the structure that reacts an impact as separate facts.

For a transfer, follow the piece through narrowing, turning, orientation and staging. Each imposed constraint should remove an unwanted degree of freedom without adding an over-constrained state. An unpowered surface can be useful guidance or the dominant drag source. An agitator can release a bridge or repeatedly throw the piece away from the receiving contact. A funnel and a singulator solve different problems. Their useful rate must be evaluated at full, partial and nearly empty inventory, including an interrupted feed and a reverse.

For a shooter, identify the entry state, compression history, contact duration, wheel surface velocities, release angle and resulting translation and spin. Free wheel speed is not ball speed. A soft piece deforms and can slip; a flexible ring can enter the same nominal gap in several shapes. An additional backing roller can control spin while changing friction and packaging. The architecture should include a measured calibration process and the mechanical references that make it repeatable after service.

For a positioning mechanism, follow the force path from the piece through the end effector, joint, bearings, structure and chassis. Motor encoder accuracy does not measure output deflection or backlash. A stiff-looking plate can be attached through a flexible joint; a highly reduced gearbox can still have a weak final tooth or inadequate shaft support. Reducing mass far from an axis reduces inertia more than an equal reduction near it. Counterbalances reduce one load component while creating another angle-dependent force. State the complete motion and load condition before borrowing a ratio.

For a climber, distinguish acquisition, retention, lift, settling and power-off support. The load path changes during those phases. A hook that catches a rung is not necessarily the part that safely supports the final suspension. A winch that can lift the robot can still rotate it into an illegal or damaging contact if the chain line is far from the center of mass. Shared-joint climbs couple primary scoring damage to endgame reliability. In 2026 the strategic default remains fuel-first and low-priority climb, even when the hardware itself is interesting.

## First-order calculations are checks, not performance certifications

Surface speed is approximately `v = pi * D * RPM / 60` when diameter and time units are consistent. At the same shaft speed, changing diameter changes both surface speed and the torque needed to produce a given contact force. A reduction improves output torque while lowering output speed; a tooth-count pair must be interpreted in the team's stated driver/driven order. This corpus preserves source notation where direction is ambiguous. Do not silently invert it or turn a free-speed calculation into loaded performance.

For a rotating joint, gravity torque is approximately the sum of each mass times gravitational acceleration times its perpendicular moment arm. Dynamic torque also includes inertia times angular acceleration and friction. A long telescoping arm changes both moment arm and inertia through its stroke. A final reduction, shaft and bearing must react the load even when several motors share the input. Mechanical advantage can vary sharply through a linkage, so checking only the endpoints can miss the highest force.

Flywheel stored energy is `E = 0.5 * I * omega^2`. That explains why inertia can buffer a short launch impulse, but does not prove a heavier flywheel improves recovery or total score. Motor power must replace the average energy, and extra inertia costs spin-up energy and mass. Recovery also depends on the controller, transmission, compression and timing of the next ball. A shooter can perform well with low added inertia if its motor authority and contact state are appropriate. Preserve counterexamples rather than turning one champion's design into a universal prescription.

For a complete fuel path, the minimum capacity of its serial services provides only an optimistic ceiling. Arrival gaps, bursty supply, jams and motion can reduce output well below that minimum. A nearly empty hopper can expose a different bottleneck from a full one. Track delivered scored fuel per usable interval, not just bench BPS. For coral, track a full acquisition-to-next-acquisition cycle and the probability of a retained legal score. The fastest isolated joint motion is not automatically the fastest useful task.

## Tests should distinguish competing explanations

If an intake jams, record which contact first stops and whether a shaft, belt or guide moved. Change one compression or support dimension and reproduce the failed approach. If a shooter misses, separate localization error, hood-reference error, wheel recovery and ball-entry variation before changing the shot map. If a lift oscillates, measure both encoder tracking and physical tip motion. If an expanding hopper fails, test a loaded interrupted transition rather than only repeating empty endpoint moves.

Useful reported quantities include sample count, piece condition, battery voltage, configuration, setup and failure definition. Team-reported rates and movement times retain that label. A requirement table is not a results table; grey or unmet targets in a binder must not be imported as achievements. A CAD image is evidence of a design, not proof of a competed installation. A later rebuild must not overwrite the earlier robot. The all-125 binder audit distinguishes a located publication, accessible technical pages, a false association and an unresolved search; none establishes that every possible binder has been found.

## Recommendation output

Start with the game state and intended alliance role. State the measurable task goals, then name year/version-specific inspirations and the physical interfaces that must be redesigned. Include a positive reason and a failure mode for each major mechanism choice. Compare at least one coherent alternative under the same partner, supply, defense and development assumptions. Conclude with the smallest integrated experiment that could change the architecture decision. A recommendation that sounds fluent in team numbers but omits these conditions has not met the purpose of this database.

title: 2026-27 · Preacceleration, passive restraint and retrofit compression

# 2026-27: Preacceleration, passive restraint and retrofit compression

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The interview describes a two-X44 intake at 2.5:1, passive carbon upper roller, roller-floor transmission described as 17:19, and a 3-inch steel drum driven by four X60s with powered hood rollers. A previously powered upper feed roller was made passive after jamming. Drum-region compression is reported as 3/8 inch and final roller compression as 1/2 inch.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly connects the stepped compression to fitting a replacement shooter in the existing robot, and the passive roller change to avoiding fuel being driven downward into jams. Collector repair access is deliberate because it receives impacts.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The important reference is the sequence of contacts, not simply four launcher motors. Upstream acceleration reduces the velocity increment demanded of the drum, while the passive restraint prevents one contact from injecting fuel into an already occupied region. More powered surfaces can therefore lower useful flow. A retrofit also fixes the available path length and elevation; its compression distribution cannot safely be transplanted without the same incoming velocity and support geometry. Separately, the agitation priority hierarchy means collector deployment and automatic shooting agitation are competing commands rather than independent subsystems.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure hopper-to-exit rate and current with the upper restraint passive versus driven, at several fill levels. Check worn fuel and simultaneous agitation. Preserve the source ratio order until driver/driven orientation is verified.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

# 2026-125: Dish packaging and shooting independence require a coordinated robot

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The interview describes an eleven-position dish, front and rear vertical roller sets to clear its center, approximately 425 degrees of turret freedom, a 3-inch main shooter wheel, a 1-inch upper roller and additional feed wheels. A centrally packaged turret is a whole-robot commitment. The dish determines where modules, structure and storage can sit, and its useful capacity depends on clearing the central dead region rather than nominal perimeter volume. Turret range is only useful if localization, target selection, hood travel and cable management support it. The FMS-aware timing offset is a flight-time decision: fuel released before activation must arrive while scoring is valid. That offset is not a transferable constant without checking release-to-arrival time and the applicable game timing.

Compare central residual fuel, sustained rate and moving-shot accuracy at different turret angles. Validate the hub-state lead time against measured flight time; verify cable/swept-volume clearance over the claimed angular range.

# 2026-1114: A rising fuel path makes agitation and service mass consequential

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The collector kicker changed from a hanging deployed bar to a member that folds with the hopper. Side agitation, passive dead-zone rollers, added gripping rollers and a belt-linked roller elevator feed the drum. The retained dated source account records the climber being installed March 1 and removed March 19 before the first event.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The folding kicker is explained as improving bump clearance. Added contact surfaces respond to trapped fuel and insufficient feed. The retained team account attributes removing the climber to weight, with later mass devoted to reliable feeding.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

This design transports fuel upward before release, so every additional elevation change has a traction and packing cost. An apparently small passive roller may be important because it removes a place where the moving stream can unload into a dead pocket. The coupled hopper/kicker motion is also a route-clearance feature, not merely storage expansion. Removing a climber should be understood as reallocating mass and development effort to the bottleneck; it does not imply that tower scoring was mechanically impossible or that endgame fuel should be counted as climb value.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Log current and residual inventory along the entire rising path, test folding while fully loaded, and compare bump clearance before and after the kicker folds. Do not derive undisclosed gear ratios from the interview wording.

# 2026-1678: Protected carbon intake and continuous J-path launcher feed

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A 2×1 aluminum crash member protects a carbon intake roller. Later wrist plates use half-inch stock with raised hard-stop contact regions and pocketing. The shooter uses a J-shaped accelerating tunnel, a separate feeder, a four-X60 steel drum and powered hood rollers; its hood pivot is supported independently of the drum. Two side cameras were added to the original front Limelight.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team links the crash member to allowing a light but impact-sensitive roller, larger hard-stop contact to reduced wear, low electronics/wiring to a lower floor, and additional cameras to midfield vision gaps found at Half Moon Bay. The source also describes replacing an earlier S-shaped path after direction reversal hurt consistency.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The useful package combines structural load routing with flow continuity. The crash member must intercept contact before the carbon roller does; copying only the carbon tube removes the condition that made it practical. A lower floor reduces the climb imposed on loose fuel, while a J-path avoids reversing the velocity component that was just created upstream. Independent hood support can reduce parasitic coupling, but hood and drum still need controlled compression over their complete angle range. The camera change is evidence that good scoring performance near the hub did not guarantee adequate pose observability in midfield.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure path velocity and compression through hood travel, inspect crash loads with the collector extended, and compare localization availability in midfield before and after adding side views. Retain a separate shooter-ready gate before enabling the floor.

# 2026-1690: Precondition fuel before a compact turret, then manage defended stability

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The interview describes eleven active carbon/silicone floor rollers powered by an X60 through a stated 2:1 reduction, with 3-mm-pitch GT2 inter-roller belts. A later acceleration stage is described as delivering approximately 8 m/s with near-zero incoming spin. Compact turret packaging shares shafts and places hood-drive hardware to limit diameter. A defended shooting mode cancels shooting on the move.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly cites efficiency at small pulley radii for its belt choice and compactness for the turret transmission layout. Its defended mode is explained as planting the robot to resist being pushed and emptying more accurately.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Preconditioning is a useful way to separate high-volume transport from precision release. A turret receiving fuel with controlled velocity and spin needs to add less correction, but it inherits errors in every upstream roller and transfer gap. The reported 8 m/s is an internal-stage claim, not a measured final trajectory specification or match-average rate. A planted mode also shows why turret capability does not require moving continuously: the best control mode depends on contact conditions. A future implementation must budget traction and battery demand for both upstream acceleration and chassis resistance.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure entrance velocity/spin distribution, current at each stage, and accuracy under controlled lateral contact. Compare planted and moving modes with the same fuel condition and load rather than ranking them from an undefended demo.

# 2026-1706: Twin spindexers trade packaging freedom for multiple coupled interfaces

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The mechanism has two rotating floor/cone systems and uptake ramps, separately controlled kickers, independent turrets and hood adjustment. The interview describes X44-driven indexer systems, 6-inch aluminum flywheels replacing heavy steel trials, an under-mounted battery on a pinned removable panel, and chassis-speed-dependent intake voltage bounded around 6.5–12 V.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

Aluminum flywheels were chosen after the steel trial proved too heavy. The battery mounting responds to crowded internal packaging. The retained interview account describes bristles, stacked wheels and shaped cones as successive feed iterations.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Two aiming channels do not automatically double match output. Fuel must be distributed to both cones, delivered through both ramps and accelerated without one path starving or overpacking. Moving-shot math must use the location of each turret rather than a single robot-center vector; angular chassis motion creates different local velocities at separated release points. Dynamic collector speed can match acquisition to chassis motion, but the exact speed signal and interpolation should be checked in code because the caption wording mixes angular and translational quantities. The removable battery panel is part of the architecture: dense packaging is only useful if the robot can still be serviced reliably.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test unequal hopper loading, one jammed lane, low battery, turning shots and underbody battery retention after bump contact. Verify the actual intake-speed input in source code before reproducing the controller.

# 2026-1768: Rebuild removes feed compression and separates shooter readiness

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The interview distinguishes a former divided two-lane/double-spindexer arrangement from the drum rebuild with a roller floor. A powered lower intake roller was replaced by two 3/4-inch aluminum shafts with reduced compression. Compliant wheels near entry feed a J-shaped path; a guide was added after WPI wobble. Four motors drive the drum/kicker/hood group, and feed is enabled only after aiming, speed and hood conditions are satisfied.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team reports improved throughput after reducing collector compression, adds the guide to control observed motion, and describes reduced belt tension as a current-draw improvement. Driver controls were intentionally simplified around repeatable actions.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

This is evidence against treating maximum grip as maximum throughput. Too many opposing powered contacts can trap deformable fuel or make its entry velocity inconsistent. Removing a roller changes the entire force chain, so the improvement should not be generalized to a collector with different ground geometry. Likewise, the software shoot command is a sequencer rather than a simultaneous motor-on command. Feeding early can pull down wheel speed or create an inaccurate initial volley, while waiting unnecessarily long reduces usable shift time.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Compare feed latency, initial-volley accuracy, current and residual fuel with the actual readiness tolerances. Inspect the added guide over hood travel and repeat reduced-compression tests with worn fuel.

# 2026-2481: Large inventory changes collector loading, frame clearance and drive gearing

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The interview reports approximately 115-fuel capacity, a 33.5×21.375-inch robot envelope before the described extension, a wide 3-inch two-X60 intake, a load shield above the collector, and hopper structure changed from angle to tube. A two-position hood changed from pneumatic to linear actuation; wheel speed covers intermediate distances. Custom modules allow ratio changes and were geared down for the loaded robot.

The second collector motor and load shield respond to stalling and hopper pressure. Tube structure responds to racking and snagging. The lower drive ratio is explicitly tied to moving a heavily loaded robot across bumps with less stalling/current; the source attributes the actuator change to weight.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Capacity is useful only if it remains mobile and unloads reliably. A large stored column presses on its lowest contact surfaces, so a shield can be more valuable than another nominally faster roller. The hopper bar cutout and wheel sizing belong to the same route-clearance problem: a robot that can collect a full load but beaches on the bump loses the strategic value of that load. Two hood positions simplify mechanism travel, but the remaining range must be supplied by speed without creating unacceptable release-angle or recovery-time sensitivity.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test acceleration, bump traversal, braking, tip margin and current at empty/half/full inventory. Measure sustained unload rate rather than dividing nominal capacity by the fastest initial volley. Verify exact dimensions and the source gear notation in CAD.

# 2026-6369: A drum rebuild shifts the problem to inertia, loading and inspection mass

Likewise, a removed climber is an unfielded feature for the filmed configuration, not an autonomous capability.

# 2026-7558: Surface contamination, inertia and power control interact

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The collector deploy angle was flattened after first-event jams. The retained interview account describes surgical tubing replaced by grippier floor surfaces after fuel debris caused slip. A material choice can work with clean practice fuel yet fail when loose surface debris changes friction. A flywheel can smooth a transient without fixing an inadequate recharge rate or a hot motor. The useful design reference is therefore a tested material/contact path plus an explicit electrical budget, not a motor count. Robot logging should distinguish commanded voltage, actual bus voltage, current limit, speed error and fuel flow; otherwise starvation and electrical saturation can look like the same shooting symptom.

body:
# 2026-7769: Passive feed solved one jam while rack durability remained unresolved

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The rack collector and belt floor feed an originally divided shooter that became one continuous drum. In the team’s later technical discussion, powered upper/lower indexing rollers overpacked the ramp; immobilizing the lower rollers corrected that feed issue. The static hood avoids an exposed powered-roller belt. The team separately reports repeated polycarbonate rack-tooth failures and a 45-A deploying/5-A deployed current-limit strategy at Worlds.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The stated priorities are simple, durable mechanisms and resistance to trench contact. The lower surface was made static to meter entry rather than forcing fuel into a congested ramp. The current-limit change aimed to let the intake collapse under impact; failures became less frequent but did not disappear.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

This example needs two distinct failure histories. A feed-path change can be successful while the deployment structure remains unreliable. Stronger propulsion is not automatically the fix for a packing jam, and a high-performing alliance run does not certify rack durability. Source-reported storage also has a useful distinction: almost 70 geometric capacity versus commonly 50–60 in play. Protected interior PETG vector wheels surviving a season is not evidence that the same prints would survive as exposed intake wheels.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test the passive lower feed with full hopper pressure and varied fuel. Instrument deployment impact/current and inspect tooth-root damage. A proposed decoupling of intake sides is a future idea, not a fielded fix.

## Limits

Focused interview plus first-party technical replies 5, 8, 11, 13 and 15 in topic 521008. Tech-slide access returned Gone; the slides were not reviewed or counted as a binder.

# 2026-9128: Trench access and speed-error feeding explain the rebuild

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A slotted three-roller transfer provides adjustable compression before a two-X60 high-inertia launcher. The flexible Hopper Flopper compresses under the trench and re-expands afterward. The shooter was reversed relative to the original robot, and the feeder speed varies with launcher speed error. The interview explicitly reports no climb.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team links trench access to losing neutral-zone fuel races, preserving capacity to avoiding a smaller fixed hopper, and reversed orientation to reducing the need to turn after acquisition. Transfer modulation is intended to give fuel sufficient energy transfer while maintaining accuracy.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A compliant storage envelope changes which routes are available, so its value cannot be measured only in added fuel. It can change autonomous arrival order and the opponent’s available supply. Speed-error-dependent feed is a form of demand management: slow entry when the launcher is behind instead of allowing a nominally high feed command to create low-energy misses. The caption’s flywheel mass arithmetic is inconsistent, so preserve the qualitative high-inertia claim and seek a published mass breakdown rather than silently choosing one number.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Compare route arrival times, full-load trench passage, recovery after contact, and total scored fuel with fixed versus variable feeding. Measure sustained and initial BPS separately.

## Limits

Interview plus team replies in topic 515730. The first release reports about 15–16 BPS over a full roughly 80-fuel hopper versus around 20–25 initially; these are team reports for that configuration, not measurements of every later revision.

# 2026-9496: A fixed-angle launcher deliberately shifts complexity elsewhere

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

The passive deployment also makes initial orientation and autonomous motion part of the mechanism’s operation. A simple subsystem can therefore demand careful whole-match planning without being a poor design.

title: 2026-5687 · Capstan deployment and belt-floor lanes are dated fixes, not universal upgrades
body:
# 2026-5687: Capstan deployment and belt-floor lanes are dated fixes, not universal upgrades

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

First-party replies describe 2-inch upper rollers, a 1.25-inch lower roller and about half an inch of compression. The robot changed from roller floor to belt floor between URI and UVM, and from rack deployment to a rope capstan after tooth damage. A 6-inch, 1/8-inch-wall aluminum drum was urethane-coated, machined and balanced; its reported inertia is a little over 80 lb·in².

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team says lower collector compression reduced motor bogging. It reports lower current and faster feeding after the belt-floor change; belt spacing created lanes and reduced fuel spinning in place. Rope deployment addressed rack tooth failures, with rope tension becoming the continuing adjustment.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

This is a useful counterexample to choosing a floor from appearance alone. Belt spacing can organize deformable fuel and remove an unproductive rotating contact state, but that result depends on piece size, belt spacing, load and friction. A capstan cannot skip discrete gear teeth, yet it can slip, stretch, lose tension or suffer anchor damage. The team’s prior capstan experience also changes development risk: the decision was supported by an existing implementation history rather than an untested mechanism adopted casually midseason.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test lane stability, residual fuel, electrical demand and rope tension after repeated impacts. Preserve the report that auto shot timers shortened by over half a second without inventing exact before/after BPS.

## Limits

Selected first-party replies 14, 16, 21, 23, 38, 40 and 42 in topic 515683, plus code-release topic 524737. This is a discussion/code-release review, not a reviewed technical binder.

body:
# 2026-9483: Small turret throughput cannot be inferred from exterior geometry

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

First-party replies describe separate X44s for indexer and spindexer, a spinning floor/cone with no deliberate wall compression, and multiple feeder-wheel and ratio trials. The third intake version adds a kicker and movable secondary kicker. The shooter lacks an upper roller; its moving-shot solution combines tuned lookup data and a physics calculation that compensates for spin.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team says the movable kicker resolves earlier collector difficulty and clarifies that the feeder delivers fuel without spin. It does not provide a definitive causal explanation for all of the achieved spindexer throughput. The added flood light helps close-range tag reliability rather than substantially increasing long-range detection.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The absence of a counter-roller makes spin an explicit aiming input rather than something to assume away. A compact turret may leave more free hopper area, but the detailed explanation of dead zones and geometry offered by another commenter is expressly an outsider’s hypothesis. Keep that hypothesis separate from the team’s replies. Successful self-unjamming also does not mean jams never occur; the source explicitly acknowledges occasional jams.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure entrance spin and moving-shot error across turret angles, record jam/recovery frequency and time, and inspect exact CAD before copying clearances or interpreting an image-based diameter estimate.

## Limits

Selected first-party replies 26, 30, 33, 35 and 47 in topic 515383. Reply 44 is outside analysis, not team intent or a CAD inspection.

# 2025-111: Floor supply changes the mechanism without replacing the scoring arm

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A floor collector was added after Northern Lights while the elevator/arm architecture remained. The retained account identifies roughly 16 pounds of added collector mass, offset by lighter carriage/effector parts. Internal rollers retain coral while the mechanism holds it inverted during algae acquisition. Coral and algae contact regions are offset by about six inches.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly identifies difficult station alignment under defense and successful floor pickups on 1778/2046 as motivations. The offset is described as allowing algae removal and coral placement in one fluid transition.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A floor collector should be evaluated as a new cycle source, not an isolated pickup demo. The existing arm must keep coral controlled through the algae motion, and mass must be recovered elsewhere without creating excessive compliance. The six-inch separation is an interface dimension for that combined motion; it is not a universal clearance between any two manipulators.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Compare defended station cycles with complete floor-to-score cycles, including failed pickups and inverted retention. Check whether the mass-saving parts preserve L4 accuracy and fatigue life.

# 2025-180: Self-deploying acquisition still requires indexed possession

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

Multiple sensors provide intermediate possession states instead of equating “something entered” with “ready to score.” A combined coral/algae mechanism must also preserve the retained object through rotation, not just when stationary.

# 2025-190: Funnel closure and adaptive grip are separate control problems

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A retroreflective beam across the station funnel detects entry and triggers closure before coral rolls to the end effector. An extending roller acquires ground algae. The retained scoring assembly uses an elevator and arm; the climb deploys with a gas shock and captures the cage while the robot advances.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The interview describes varying algae-holding voltage using current-related feedback, with more effort when the piece is farther out and less after it is seated. Exact thresholds are not supplied.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

An entry beam establishes interruption, not orientation or secure final possession. The handoff therefore needs additional state and a recovery path. Adaptive grip can reduce unnecessary loading after capture, but current also changes with friction, compression and voltage; it cannot be treated as a direct position measurement without calibration. The gas-shock climb similarly depends on a defined hard stop and a controlled chassis approach.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Induce partial entry and bounced coral, measure algae retention at different compression and current, and verify cage capture over realistic lateral offsets.

# 2025-359: A telescoping arm avoids a handoff but moves a large work envelope

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The interview describes four shoulder motors with a stated 111:1 reduction, a chain-driven dead-axis pivot, and a two-motor telescoping arm. Its wide collector uses front/back roller groups and aluminum centering guides to acquire differently oriented coral; rigid guide plates reflect coral’s low compressibility. The retained record describes extending stage length for L4/net reach.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team links the multi-motor shoulder to power demand. Its acquisition geometry is intended to bring floor coral into the same mechanism that scores it, avoiding a separate transfer.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Eliminating a handoff trades transfer risk for arm inertia, sweep clearance and control burden. Extension changes both shoulder torque and the position of the robot’s loaded center of mass. A floor hard stop can define a repeatable pickup plane, but should not be confused with clearance throughout the rest of the motion. Thin coral tolerates less forced compression than foam fuel, so roller selection must be paired with a controlled guide gap.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Map shoulder current and deflection through extension, test pickup against a wall, and verify coral control during acceleration and sudden chassis braking.

## Limits

# 2025-604: Precision depends on stiffness, backlash and feeding order

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A single-stage elevator is driven by chains on both sides to reduce twist; the arm/wrist and shimmed transmissions aim to minimize backlash. The large corrugated-plastic station funnel damps entry. Independently stopped feed rollers can hold coral while the gripper handles algae, and a compact climber fits beneath the funnel.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team explicitly treats accuracy as a mechanical and software requirement, identifies dual-sided elevator drive with resisting twist, and explains pausing coral feed during algae possession.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A vision system can command the correct pose yet miss a branch if the scoring frame deflects or the transmission reverses through backlash. Hybrid cycles add a scheduling constraint: the incoming coral must not collide with a manipulator that is still gripping algae. The funnel and climber also compete for the same physical space, so a copied climber cannot be assumed to fit behind another team’s station system.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure effector displacement under lateral load and direction reversal; test queued coral while holding algae. Compare repeatability after repeated elevator cycles and drivetrain impacts.
