title: How to Win a World Championship | FRC Strategy Analysis
body:
# How to Win a World Championship | FRC Strategy Analysis

Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU

Published: 2026-05-04. Review: 2026-10-25. Automatic English captions; 1388 timestamped segments. Every exported caption was read. The final caption begins at 46:19; this is not a video-duration measurement. No raw transcript is redistributed. No visual audit was possible.

A complete available-caption study of the upper-bracket final and all three 2026 Einstein finals. The central account is the coupling of autonomous contact, transition position, neutral-zone supply, steal timing, shoot-on-the-move passing and 4065’s defensive geometry. Breakdowns and uncertain intent remain explicit confounders.

Compare whole alliance control loops, not drum rate against turret rate in isolation. A robot can make a smaller immediate score while changing who owns the next supply of fuel, who can arrive before a shift starts and which opponent must cross a defended bottleneck. The source’s counterfactual wins and point-denial estimates are hypotheses, not measured individual contributions.

## 0:07–0:35 · Scope, alliance identities and the danger of rewriting the series as a clean architecture contest

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=7s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The introduction treats the upper-bracket meeting plus three finals as one strategic series. Daly fields 4065, 4414 and 1323; Newton fields 868, 2046 and 2910. The creator credits both Daly’s scoring pair and 4065’s defense. Later passages explicitly describe interruptions to 1323, 868 and 2046. The account therefore contains several changing robot-availability states rather than four repetitions of the same six healthy machines.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

An architecture comparison should condition on operational state. A two-turret alliance beating two dumpers in the final result does not establish an unconditional turret advantage: starting positions, autonomous contact, defensive assignments, fuel distribution and failures all change between matches. Conversely, describing the series only as breakdowns discards the account of deliberate supply control. Preserve both explanations until footage and team logs can separate them. The six active robots are the match-specific roster; a reserve on the championship alliance must not be silently treated as an active participant in these four recordings.

## 0:35–3:28 · Upper bracket: 1323’s corner cut, a disrupted 2910 auto and the 4414–4065 follow route

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=35s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator describes 1323 beginning at an angle and cutting ahead of 2910 rather than first translating sideways. He says this leaves one corner of fuel but permits a larger sweep around the pile. He attributes 2910’s later misalignment and intake corner catching to the rotation caused by that encounter. On the other side, 4414 makes a central pass with a following 4065 route, collects near the hub wall and returns to score from the outpost side. He connects 4414’s net and hopper to retaining a large collection across the bump and clearing it before autonomous ends. His belief that the teams timed the opposing routes is explicitly an assumption.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

The useful design requirement is an autonomous system whose acquisition envelope, collision recovery and route compatibility are evaluated together. A route can abandon a small pocket yet improve total possession by reaching a more valuable arc first. A high collection rate can create an exit-path problem if the loaded robot cannot traverse the selected obstacle without shedding fuel. A net is therefore part of the mobility–storage interface, not an isolated capacity feature. None of this gives a dimension, actual retained count or certified causal diagnosis of 2910’s auto error. Reproduce the route interaction with synchronized overhead video and logs before concluding that the same cut always defeats the same opponent.

## 3:28–5:14 · Upper bracket transition: where the defender ends autonomous determines which ten seconds it can influence

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=208s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The account praises 4065 for ending near midfield and immediately reaching across to contest Newton’s transition fuel. It contrasts 868 ending deeper on its own side and arriving after 1323 and 4414 have already collected and moved ahead of it. The commentator argues that a defender arriving late misses a short opportunity to reduce the autonomous winner’s transition scoring. He describes Daly converting its uncontested collection into sustained transition output.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Treat autonomous terminal pose as the initial condition of teleop, including the defender. Maximizing a small autonomous contribution may be a poor trade if it places that robot too far from the next high-value interception. The source describes a timing window, not a universal instruction to send a defender immediately across the field. The outcome depends on the actual active-hub schedule, legal routes, expected collector arrival and whether intercepting one scorer leaves a partner free. Official fuel confirms a 65–30 transition advantage for Daly in this match, but that alliance total cannot measure the individual value of 4065’s terminal pose or prove the stated cause.

## 5:14–9:00 · Upper bracket first active shifts: dual moving passers clean supply while imposing incidental delay

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=314s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator describes 1323 and 4414 splitting the neutral zone, circling through fuel and passing it back while their hub is inactive. They also occupy enough of 2046’s path to make acquisition awkward. He contrasts this with a dumper stopping to pass a batch. In his account, 2046 finds little fuel in the neutral zone, returns toward its own corner reserves and later has difficulty obtaining another hopper. He mentions 868 holding fuel and a 4065 blocker delaying part of 2910’s final discharge.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

This is a coupled acquisition, passing and interference role. Passing while moving can let an off-shift robot keep collecting instead of serializing collect, stop, orient and release; the same motion can close an opponent’s useful approach. That does not make every turret a good moving passer. Intake throughput, feed continuity, aiming under motion, range, loaded acceleration and the ability to keep fuel on the intended side all matter. Fuel temporarily held in a third robot is another supply state, even if that robot scores little. The source supplies neither a complete fuel ledger nor timing measurements, so avoid turning this account into a quantified claim that turrets always clean the field faster than drums.

## 9:00–13:47 · Upper bracket: starvation changes departure location, which changes the next steal and partner release

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=540s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The analysis follows 2046 from an unproductive neutral-zone visit into a corner collection, then into a later cross-field steal. It says the later departure gives 1323 roughly three additional seconds before the steal arrives. In the other direction, 4414 can leave earlier to remove Newton’s stashed fuel. Later, 1323 screens 868 so 4414 can cross back, while 2046 again arrives late. The creator frames these actions as compounding consequences of the earlier neutral-zone cleanup, not independent isolated tricks.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Track location and inventory at every shift boundary. A robot with the same amount of fuel but a different terminal position can have a very different next assignment. Supply denial may first force a detour, then postpone a steal, then expose a partner’s prepared pile; simply counting immediate defended scoring seconds misses those downstream opportunities. The reported three-second gain remains an estimate from edited commentary. Alternative explanations include traffic, operator choice and recovery from previous contact. An auditable event log should separate observed departure, observed arrival, unknown fuel count and inferred causal link, rather than give one long causal sentence the status of a directly observed fact.

## 13:47–16:07 · Upper bracket finish: attacking a prepared corner can matter more than another neutral-zone lap

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=827s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

Near the end of the first match analysis, the creator praises 4414 for taking fuel from a Newton corner. He argues that this forces 2046 into another neutral-zone trip instead of short local cycles. He also describes 2910 passing to replenish its own side. His explanation is that the dual turrets can continue hunting scattered fuel while moving, whereas the dumper pair loses efficiency when it can no longer fill efficiently before returning to a firing position.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

A hopper-full shooter rate is not the marginal match rate when the remaining fuel is dispersed. Distinguish release-limited, collection-limited and route-limited phases. A high-rate drum can still be strategically excellent if partners prepare dense piles or clear crossings; a moving turret can still be slow if each remaining pickup is difficult. The official upper-bracket data also limits the story: Daly leads auto 186–83 and transition 65–30, but Newton scores more in its second own active shift, 173–97, and the final period, 176–145. The source’s supply-control account should not be rewritten as Daly winning every phase. Each alliance’s own active-shift totals occur at different wall-clock periods.

## 16:07–17:41 · Non-match interval and source chronology

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=967s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

This interval is a merchandise segment between the upper-bracket analysis and finals 1. It contains no additional match tactics. The source then resumes with the first final at 17:41. The introduction and outro frame the video as a post-Worlds analysis rather than a kickoff prediction.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Recording this boundary prevents a source-navigation timestamp inside an advertisement from being mistaken for a match observation. It also preserves the difference between what was proposed before an event and what was explained afterward with knowledge of the result. No mechanism specification or match fact is extracted from this interval.

## 17:41–22:00 · Finals 1: a successful Newton auto, 1323’s reported beaching and 4414’s deliberately deferred scoring

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=1061s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator says 2910 completes its path without the previous contact, but explicitly does not know whether the route was changed. He reports 1323 becoming beached and says 4065’s planned autonomous depends partly on 1323 returning. Daly loses auto. Instead of using the transition to return and match Newton’s immediate scoring, 4414 stays collecting in the neutral zone. The creator praises this as taking supply while the other robots are occupied scoring, then returning with a fuller load for the first own active shift. He speculates that healthy Daly could use the same approach successfully after an autonomous loss.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

This is evidence against a policy that always maximizes every currently scoreable second. Giving up immediate fuel can buy the next load and remove the opponent’s future load. The official record makes the trade concrete: Daly has zero transition fuel while Newton has 57; it is not evidence that the collection produced transition points. Daly later has 83 and 117 in its own active shifts and 140 in the final period, but loses 456–518. That result neither proves the delayed-scoring choice bad nor validates the creator’s healthy-robot counterfactual. A comparison must hold failures and opponent responses constant, which this single match cannot do.

## 22:00–27:43 · Finals 1: reciprocal defense, trench firing and a changing failure state

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=1320s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The account highlights 4065’s route denial and blocker, 868 punishing a 4414 steal, and 2910 returning to the neutral zone to recycle fuel while reducing what 4414 can acquire. It says Newton uses a trench-side firing position to reduce how much of a fuel stream 4065 can obstruct. The commentator reports 1323 briefly resuming before stopping again, later problems on 2046 and a nonfunctional 868. He credits Newton’s earlier lead and supply control with surviving those late issues.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Do not attach one permanent role or health label to a robot for the whole match. A returning robot can change supply competition even before it scores, and a stopped defender changes its partner’s exposure. Trench-side firing is a reported geometry adaptation, not a certified blocked-shot percentage. The source also guesses why a team avoids another steal; without driver testimony, the safer statement is that the steal was not taken and that a defender had previously delayed that route. The match audit should locate the first missed opportunity, each recovery interval and actual scoring frame before assigning a failure mechanism or making a claim about how much closer the score would have been.

## 27:43–32:18 · Finals 2: 2046’s improved transition position creates an immediate gain and a later supply trade

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=1663s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator reports another disrupted 2910 auto and an improved 2046 finishing position ahead of 4414. In his account, 2046 collects the next fuel first and forces 4414 back to the neutral zone earlier. He estimates several seconds of 4414 scoring were denied, while admitting he does not know its exact rate. He then describes 1323 and 4414 cleaning the middle, 4065 keeping 2910 out, and 2046 spending much of its active shift obtaining and returning with one load. The quoted shift clocks go from about 22 seconds remaining at neutral-zone arrival to about eight when scoring resumes.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

A locally successful adjustment can create a later disadvantage: sending fuel rapidly through the hub and vacating the middle can give the inactive alliance a collection opportunity. Do not convert the commentator’s rough three-to-four-second estimate into 36–40 independently verified points. A defensible estimate needs actual feed activity, counted scored fuel, clock alignment and a counterfactual path. The official finals-2 table records Daly leading in auto, transition, both own active shifts and final-period fuel. The final-period edge is only 169–165, so the series story should retain the narrow late fuel difference alongside the larger earlier advantages and the 40 penalty points received by Daly.

## 32:18–36:30 · Finals 2: stealing, holding fuel and the price of trapping a cleanup robot

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=1938s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

With little safe supply at home and contested supply in the middle, the creator describes 4414 stealing. Newton responds by bringing 868 back to delay its escape. He says a pin produces penalties, but argues the delay prevents 4414 cleaning the middle, pulls another Daly robot to help and allows Newton collection or scoring. He then notes that 2910 sometimes chooses passing and supply removal instead of trying another defended scoring cycle, while 868 keeps fuel in its hopper largely to deny it. He acknowledges uncertainty about whether Newton consciously reasoned through every consequence he describes.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Evaluate holding fuel as inventory denial with a duration and opportunity cost, not automatically as scoring capacity. Removing fuel from the shared pool can hurt both alliances; its value depends on who can still score from prepared reserves, who has to search and how many active seconds remain. The creator’s judgment that a foul was worth it is not rule advice or a measured net benefit. Keep the official penalty amount separate from inferred tactical value and verify the relevant rule and referee application before discussing legality. The possible partner-release effect is a useful audit target, but cannot be assigned a point value from the final score alone.

## 36:30–38:23 · Finals 2 rewind: 4065 defends the route and the available rotation space

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=2190s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator rewinds specifically to follow 4065. He describes patient marking that does not chase 2910’s feints, with 2910’s back corners near the bump and its intake constrained by the trench bar or hub if it rotates either way. In this account, 2910 has to back away and try a different crossing, then still faces the blocker. The creator argues that denying the entrance for much of a shift reduces 2910 to approximately one hopper instead of the larger output it might otherwise deliver.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

This is the most mechanism-specific defensive hypothesis in the source: the opponent’s deployed collector and chassis envelope interact with fixed field geometry, reducing its escape motions. A blocker also changes the shot after a crossing succeeds. The implication is to test loaded and deployed geometry under contact, including reverse escape, rather than optimize only unobstructed sprint speed. It does not prove a square footprint is categorically bad or establish an exact lost hopper count. Actual turning clearance, compliance, driver visibility and legal contact need footage and geometry. A technically useful audit would record which routes are physically inaccessible versus merely slower or discouraged.

## 38:23–41:00 · Finals 3: a swapped autonomous matchup and transition congestion

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=2303s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The source describes 2910 starting opposite 4414 and 2046 opposite 1323, avoiding another 2910–1323 corner-cut encounter. It says 2046’s auto then works and 4414 reaches farther toward the middle. The commentator explicitly cannot tell whether 4414 changed its path deliberately or simply faced a different interaction. He describes 868 and another Newton robot becoming congested near the corner, leaving 1323 and 4414 a largely uncontested transition collection and discharge.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Matchup selection is part of autonomous architecture: an identical robot and path can face a very different acquisition contest when the opposing starter changes. Preserve the source’s uncertainty about a deliberate path revision. Official fuel supports a strong Daly transition, 70–13, after a much closer 177–153 auto. That does not certify which Newton robot caused congestion or establish that every second of the deficit came from it. The audit should align all six starting positions, actual collisions, the first post-auto route choice and scoring onset before attributing the 57-fuel transition difference to a single maneuver.

## 41:00–46:19 · Finals 3: reported 2046 shooting trouble, 868 damage and 4065’s handoff between targets

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Cm-RuiSNlU&t=2460s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator says 2046 can collect but its farther shots fall short, later scoring more successfully from closer range. He describes damage to 868’s turret while it continues defending. Meanwhile both Daly scorers steal when the neutral zone is empty. He singles out a 4065 move: leave a line on 2046, shift out of the trench and rotate into 2910’s approach, disrupting the arriving load. 4414’s earlier interference is said to buy time for that switch. The creator also praises staggered return sweeps by 1323 and 4414 so one can collect fuel returned by the other’s scoring.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

The causal diagnosis of 2046’s shooting problem remains unknown; “lacked power” is an interpretation, not a voltage, current or RPM log. Damage to 868 must likewise be timed and visually confirmed. The strategic account has two distinct concepts worth retaining: a scorer can buy a defender time to change targets, and partners can stagger collection to avoid competing for the same returned fuel. Neither requires claiming exact denied hoppers. Official fuel shows the decisive pre-endgame disparity: Daly’s own active shifts total 311 versus Newton’s 79; the final period is 154–161. Both alliances have zero recorded tower points. The outcome supports a fuel-and-access investigation, while the transcript and scores cannot by themselves separate mechanical interruption from defense, supply and operator decisions.

## Questions for verification

- In the upper-bracket final, how could 1323’s autonomous corner cut affect both 2910’s auto and 2046’s later steal arrival? Which links are reported and which are causal interpretation?
- Why did the creator praise 4414 for collecting during the transition in finals 1, when that choice produced zero recorded transition fuel for Daly?
- Explain how finals 2 can contain a useful Newton starvation adaptation while still being a Daly win. What role does 4065 play in that account?
- What changed in Newton’s starting matchups for finals 3, and what remains unknown about whether 4414 deliberately changed its autonomous path?
- How does the bump–trench–hub geometry constrain a square dumper’s rotation under pressure? What evidence is still required before recommending a particular footprint?
- Why can the 154–161 final-period fuel comparison in finals 3 coexist with a 306-point final margin? Why is neither number a climb comparison?
- Which exact claims about 868, 1323 and 2046 are operational observations reported by the commentator, and which would require electrical or mechanical logs to diagnose?

## Remaining uncertainties

- No match footage rendered during this pass. All described movements below are the commentator’s account, not independently observed events.
- Automatic captions repeatedly render 1323 as 3023, 3213, 3013 or 3323 and 4065 as 465 or 4090. Team identifiers in the paraphrases are normalized against the match rosters and context; this does not repair every ambiguous spoken reference.
- The creator sometimes guesses prescouting intent, a battery/power explanation, what a driver saw, or what would have happened without a breakdown. Those claims need team records or visual corroboration.
- Video timestamps index edited commentary, with pauses and rewinds. They are not match elapsed times. A reported shift-clock value is not automatically aligned to an exact broadcast frame.
- Fuel denied, hopper fills, scoring seconds and the value of penalties are not independently counted. Do not use the source’s rough rate multiplication as a measured defense statistic.
- The claim that fully operational Daly would still win after losing auto is a counterfactual. Finals 1 is confounded by reported operational problems on both alliances.
- A blocker contacting fuel, a scorer being forced off line and a mechanism failing are different causes of lost output. The transcript cannot isolate their individual effects.
review_scope: New complete read of every available timestamped caption in the browser export, including non-match intervals. Detailed paraphrase and conditional analysis; no visual footage audit. Timestamp coverage ends at the last caption start, not certified media duration.

title: How 254 beat their California counterparts at the World Championship! | FRC Strategy Analysis
body:
# How 254 beat their California counterparts at the World Championship! | FRC Strategy Analysis

Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM

Published: 2026-08-14. Review: 2026-10-25. Automatic English captions; 934 timestamped segments. Every exported caption was read. The final caption begins at 34:06; this is not a video-duration measurement. No raw transcript is redistributed. No visual audit was possible.

A complete available-caption study of 2026 Einstein match 3 (Curie–Milstein) and match 6 (Milstein–Johnson). The retrospective connects tall-dumper throughput to crossing risk, neutral-zone control, coordinated steals, 4946’s rounded perimeter and 6324’s flexible screening role. Its “lose auto by one” thesis is a conditional hypothesis, not a settled rule.

Architecture determines the set of routes available at a particular loaded configuration. Extended storage can turn a trench-capable robot into a bump-only robot during the exact interval when a steal requires escape. A partner that clears a crossing can be worth more than another marginal load, but the value depends on current inventory, shift timing and the defender’s recovery. Test these interactions as an alliance system.

## 0:07–1:40 · A retrospective organized around two different mobility and capacity contests

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=7s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator returns during the offseason to discuss two Einstein matches. He introduces 2481 as a tall, high-capacity dumper that wants a large neutral-zone collection followed by two substantial discharges per shift. He immediately pairs that scoring potential with crossing limitations and the maneuvering demands of a rectangular robot. The first example is Curie’s 8613, 6800 and 254 against Milstein’s 4915, 2481 and 1678. The second compares Milstein with Johnson’s 6324, 4946 and 2337.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Keep archetype and role separate. A high-capacity robot may be its alliance’s main scorer, but how it is supplied and escorted determines whether capacity becomes scored fuel. Do not extract “tall dumper is bad” from a source that repeatedly praises its output and shows several close contests. This is an outcome-aware retrospective: its explanation of why a plan worked is useful evidence of the creator’s theory, but cannot establish what the teams intended at the time or what an early-season design team could confidently predict.

## 1:40–4:06 · Match 3 autonomous: a collection route, a block and an unrelated failure interact

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=100s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The account describes 6800 taking a deep collection arc, 254 contesting 1678, and 8613 meeting 2481 so 2481 cannot reach the desired fuel. It separately reports 4915 getting jammed on its own trench, leaving a planned collection area untouched. The creator assumes Curie specifically prepared the autonomous interaction against 2481, but offers no team statement. In his account, Milstein loses the autonomous advantage on which its tall-dumper plan usually relies.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Three mechanisms of reduced output must remain distinct: fuel taken first by an opponent, movement constrained by another robot and a partner failing to execute its own route. The official auto fuel, Curie 188 versus Milstein 118, confirms an alliance difference; it cannot allocate the 70-fuel margin to those causes. To audit the anti-auto claim, align actual starting poses and compare earlier routes before and after the alleged change. The source’s confidence about prescouting is a hypothesis. A fast deep sweep also requires loaded exit clearance, not just reaching the pile first.

## 4:06–6:50 · Match 3 transition and first shift: filling longer can put a bump-only robot on the wrong side of the defense

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=246s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator praises Milstein for using the transition to fill rather than immediately mirror scoring. He says 1678 opens its hopper into a configuration that relies on the bump, using the briefly uncontested middle to collect more. However, 2481 is delayed filling after Curie’s earlier collection and is still in a vulnerable approach when Curie returns. The commentary describes Curie collecting and passing the middle while making 2481 and 1678’s return difficult, reducing their useful active cycles.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

The relevant state is not simply “can use the trench” on a specification sheet. It is whether the currently expanded, loaded robot can use it during the next escape. Larger storage changes both potential discharge and the route set. Staying to fill the last portion of a hopper can be costly if the defender reaches the crossing first; leaving partially full can preserve more active scoring time. This is a conditional scheduling trade, not an instruction to abandon capacity. Record fill level as unknown unless it is counted, and compare expected additional fuel with the distribution of return delays under the actual defense.

## 6:50–9:28 · Match 3 division of labor: 1678 steals while 2481 wants dense supply and 4915 cleans

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=410s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

As Curie scores its prepared fuel, the creator describes 1678 stealing rather than competing with 2481 for the remaining neutral-zone supply. He argues a trench-capable configuration makes that assignment less vulnerable to 8613 denying a bump crossing. He also describes 4915 functioning as a turret cleanup passer. He briefly judges Milstein’s prepared field state potentially competitive because fuel is held in hoppers and corners, then describes 254 slipping past an attempted interception to remove a prepared corner pile.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

A fuel map should include prepared reserves, robot inventory and which robot can legally and physically reach each reserve. A pile’s value is conditional on the route to it surviving the opponent’s next action. This is why a snapshot of potential points is not a score forecast. The creator’s approximate hundreds of waiting points are not an independently counted inventory. A mobility advantage can make the same robot the preferred thief in one configuration and a poor thief when its hopper is extended, so retrieval must include configuration and match phase rather than attach one permanent stealing role to a team number.

## 9:28–12:20 · Match 3 coordinated steals and a temporary scoring sacrifice to release the defender

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=568s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The source describes 254 and 6800 stealing from different sides, then resuming pressure on Milstein’s neutral-zone returns. Later, 2481 goes deep to steal. The commentator disagrees with giving that job to a bump-only robot when 1678 is available, while admitting he does not know the team’s reason. He says 254 suspends a scoring cycle long enough to slow 2481’s exit and allow 8613 to arrive. He cannot determine whether the resulting apparent hold is a pin because the camera does not show the necessary contact clearly.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

This is a relay between a scorer and defender: the scorer need not hold an opponent indefinitely if a brief delay lets a better-positioned partner take over. The cost is the scorer’s immediate lost output; the possible benefit is denying a much longer opponent return and freeing the scorer afterward. Neither is quantified here. The source’s uncertainty about pinning is essential evidence, not a caveat to strip off. Even a complete broadcast review may leave the contact occluded; another angle or the official foul record may be needed, and absence of a call is not a general interpretation of the rule.

## 12:20–16:14 · Match 3 finish: storage remains valuable even when the route plan loses

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=740s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator describes 254 exploiting time bought by the delay to clean the neutral zone, 8613 continuing to interfere and 6800’s position or passing action forcing 2481 toward another bump. He is unsure whether that particular 6800 action is intentional and guesses 8613 may be losing battery performance. The conclusion praises Curie’s coordination while observing that Milstein’s fuel scoring stays competitive despite the disruption. The source’s spoken figures are not a per-robot scoring breakdown.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

The official final is Curie 717–632, with auto fuel 188–118 and subsequent fuel 529–509. Those latter values are alliance totals after auto; they must not become “2481 scored 509” or “one robot was only 20 behind.” The 20-fuel post-auto difference coexists with a 70-fuel autonomous difference. The game can reward a high-capacity architecture even in a match where an opponent exploits its routes. This is precisely why a design recommendation needs a partner plan and an anti-defense validation, rather than replacing one celebrated mechanism with another based solely on which alliance won this example.

## 16:14–19:00 · Match 6 autonomous: a close loss is the setup for a theory, not proof of an optimal policy

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=974s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

In Milstein–Johnson, the creator describes 2481 receiving a less-contested deep collection, 4915 completing its auto and 1678 cutting ahead of 2337 and toward 4946. He speculates about prescouting rather than claiming team confirmation. Milstein wins autonomous by nine fuel. The creator then introduces his thesis that losing autonomous by a very small margin may be advantageous because of the sequence of active shifts and who can control the next returned fuel.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

The nine-fuel difference is a measured alliance result, while “lose by one” is a strategic hypothesis. Do not convert a conditional argument into an instruction to throw away autonomous points or deliberately accept route failures. The hypothesis depends on the cost of the lost auto margin, expected transition production, who controls the middle when fuel returns, the ability to store supply and whether the opponent can interrupt the setup. Another alliance can win auto and still control those same states, as the Daly series account illustrates. An evaluation needs matched scenarios or a validated model rather than a win-loss anecdote.

## 19:00–21:06 · Match 6 transition: a hybrid plan and a third robot that changes jobs

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=1140s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The account describes Johnson sending 6324 to score an already loaded hopper, using 2337 for some scoring and later support, and keeping 4946 in a cleanup/passing role. The creator likes having at least one capable neutral-zone cleanup robot, while wondering whether 2337 could have spent more of the transition denying 2481. He later praises 2337 for switching among defense, a screen and small scoring contributions, rather than staying in one fixed task all match.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

The opportunity cost of transition collection depends on starting inventory. A loaded robot gains less from another collection pass and can cash in the brief scoring window; a suitable partner can still secure supply. The source therefore offers a hybrid alternative to both “everyone score now” and “everyone collect now.” It does not prove every alliance needs exactly one dedicated passer. A third robot can contribute by changing another robot’s accessible path or timing, and that effect should be evaluated alongside its own points. Visual auditing should record the order of those job changes rather than infer it from a season-average statistic.

## 21:06–26:46 · 4946’s rounded perimeter and the defender-versus-pick reversal

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=1266s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator pauses the match to discuss 4946’s rounded or semicircular bumper area. He argues it can rotate and roll around contact that would hold a flat-sided square, and distinguishes a continuous curve from a hexagon or octagon with flat faces. He also explains that a defender obstructed by 6324’s pick temporarily faces an offensive problem: it must escape the screening robot before reaching its original target. His square-on-square defense model emphasizes keeping contact faces aligned, using rotation and not overcommitting to a translational feint.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

This is an interesting mechanical hypothesis because the perimeter changes contact geometry and the moment generated by a push. It is not a proof that a rounded robot always has leverage or that polygons are always trapped. Real contact includes compliant bumpers, friction, traction limits, module directions, loaded inertia and nearby walls. A curved perimeter can also change packaging, bumper construction and available acquisition width. The transfer test should compare the complete loaded drivetrains and controlled contact angles. The pick reversal is a driver-training insight: a good defender needs escape practice as well as pursuit practice. Team intent and the exact curvature remain unverified without primary geometry and footage.

## 26:46–28:40 · 6324 trades its next fill for denying 1678’s current scoring window

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=1606s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The commentary describes 1678 attempting a steal while its hopper is extended, making it bump-only at that instant. 6324 notices and interrupts the return rather than continuing to fill itself. The creator estimates 6324 has a much smaller load and 1678 a larger one; he says the delay consumes roughly the remaining useful scoring interval. He also acknowledges that 1678 still removes fuel from Johnson and could pass or score it later, so the steal is not automatically valueless.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Value the inventories on a schedule. Removing fifty hypothetical fuel from an opponent is not the same as adding fifty score now, and a delayed load can become exposed to a reciprocal steal. Likewise, a small hopper on a support robot is not automatically a reason to defend: the partner needs a current scoring window worth protecting, and the delay must survive the opponent’s available escape. The exact hopper counts and twelve-second estimate are not independently measured. A visual event log should mark the route block, changed configuration, attempted escapes, release and actual first scoring time, with unknown counts left null.

## 28:40–30:18 · A pick, a reciprocal steal and the fact that large loaded hoppers remove fuel from the field

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=1720s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The creator describes 6324 screening to let 4946 leave while 1678 and 2481 collide or congest the middle. He then notes 6324 taking back fuel from Milstein’s side during part of its own scoring time. His explanation is that the neutral zone has become sparse partly because so much fuel is already held in 1678 and 2481. The initial Milstein steal has value, but the delayed use of that inventory allows Johnson to recover some of the supposed advantage.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

An alliance can be rich in fuel but poor in immediately accessible scoring opportunities. Large loaded hoppers reduce shared field supply for everybody, including the owner’s partners; an opponent with another reachable reserve may temporarily have the better play. This is a dynamic inventory and timing problem, not simply hopper capacity times shooter rate. The collision and screening intent still require footage. A useful agent should be able to explain why the same 6324 can screen, steal and score at different moments without collapsing those actions into a generic “support” paragraph or assuming every action was a preplanned call.

## 30:18–32:09 · A three-point final, a thirteen-point clean difference and the limits of the losing-auto thesis

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=1818s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The source closes by following Johnson’s prepared corner fuel and loaded robots, Milstein’s late effort to find reserves and both Milstein scorers returning for final cycles. He interprets the remaining supply and shift order as the reason Johnson can win despite losing auto narrowly. He also gives a no-penalty comparison of 678–691. The final recorded match is 688–691 because Milstein receives ten penalty points. The commentary’s claim that the auto loser has the better teleop conditions is an interpretation of this match state.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Preserve both margins: three in the official final, thirteen in fuel or clean output, with the penalty difference identified. This close result is sensitive to many events besides active-shift order. Compare it to the upper-bracket Daly example: there, winning auto accompanies strong transition position and cleanup that deny the opponent an easy supply setup. Here, the source argues the auto winner does not maintain that control and also faces crossing and screening problems. The transferable principle is to model the next supply state and routes under either autonomous outcome. It is not that auto has negative value, and the source does not establish a universal optimal margin.

## 32:09–34:06 · Outro, proposed future interviews and review boundary

[Source navigation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oo5nP00wVBM&t=1929s). These are commentary-video times, not match-clock times.

### Attributed source account

The outro mentions future IRI and Chezy analysis and potential coach interviews, and invites further match suggestions. The creator believes he has discussed most or all Einstein alliances by this point. That is a statement about his coverage, not a verified inventory of every match or every video on the channel.

### Conditional engineering or strategy interpretation

Do not use an outro claim to certify channel completeness. The database’s discovered-video list and canonical-match list need their own inventories, including alternate recordings and any replayed attempts. This study covers the two described canonical matches and the author’s defense theory, through the last available caption. It contains no new direct visual observations and cannot be used to clear a pending visual-audit flag.

## Questions for verification

- Why is an expanded 1678 hopper also a route constraint, and how does that change who should attempt a steal?
- How can 254 deliberately stop scoring briefly yet improve its alliance’s output later? What makes the claimed causal effect unverified?
- Why does 6324’s choice to delay a loaded 1678 differ from a generic instruction that every scorer should always defend?
- Explain the creator’s rounded-bumper hypothesis for 4946 and identify at least three reasons that a circle alone cannot guarantee escape.
- What is meant by a defender having to play offense against a partner’s pick, and what would you observe to distinguish an intentional pick from ordinary congestion?
- Compare this video’s “lose auto narrowly” thesis with the earlier Daly account of compounding an auto win. Under what different supply and route assumptions can both be reasonable?
- What are the official final and clean scores of match 6? Why must the three-point final margin not be substituted for the thirteen-point clean margin?

## Remaining uncertainties

- This is an August retrospective of May matches, with knowledge of outcomes. It is not evidence that these lessons were already consensus during kickoff or early season.
- The complete available captions were read; the underlying footage did not render. No described collision, perimeter, shot, pin or route is independently visually verified in this pass.
- The captions corrupt Curie, team names and several numbers. 6800 is Valor, 8613 is Barker, 2481 is Roboteers, 4946 is Alpha Dogs; exact identifiers are normalized only where rosters and context establish them.
- The creator estimates hoppers, potential points and delay durations, and openly guesses autonomous prescouting intent. None is an independently counted robot contribution.
- The commentary’s effective 55-second endgame groups a preceding active shift with the shared final period for one alliance. It must not replace the official final-30-second score component or the rule definition.
- The author is unsure whether an apparent hold on 2481 is a pin and cannot see the hub-side contact. Do not turn this into a legal ruling.
- Rounded-perimeter escape is a hypothesis from this interaction, not proof of immunity to defense. Traction, friction, contact normal, module torque, field obstacles and loaded mass still require examination.
- A close match after an autonomous loss cannot demonstrate that intentionally losing auto is globally optimal. The hypothesis requires comparable alliances, margin, supply-control ability and opponent response.

title: Einstein visual-audit protocol and current checkpoint
body:
# Einstein visual-audit protocol and current checkpoint

## What this edition actually establishes

The corpus contains 80 canonical Einstein match records across 2022–2026: 18, 15, 15, 16 and 16 respectively. All 80 have a candidate recording link after recovery of the official 2022 match-2 page. A canonical TBA match row is not a verified inventory of every played/replayed attempt or every camera angle. That additional completeness check remains open.

Zero visual match audits are complete. Six recording pages were opened for access/identity checks; the rest were not individually tested in this pass. Representative recordings from all five seasons supplied metadata but no decoded match frame, remaining black and buffering. Normal reload, playback controls, a lower quality on the 2022 player, seeking on the 2026 player and documented media export did not produce footage. The failure is specific to these tested sessions; it does not prove all videos are unavailable or identify a network cause. It was not a visible bot challenge in this session.

The user authorized solving the prior CAPTCHA. On opening the normal watch page there was no CAPTCHA to solve. The transcript interface worked. All eleven previously pending exports were recovered. Two new available-caption reads cover six canonical 2026 matches, with detailed attributed accounts and conditional analysis. Nine recovered exports still await full content review. The prior 33 caption studies retain their inherited review scope. Nothing in this checkpoint is represented as permanent internal model memory or as visual watching.

## Identity before tactics

Compare the title, year, teams, alliance colors, bracket position and final score. A similar title or a mirror association is insufficient. The rejected 2022 match-2 link previously pointed to match 15. The replacement is the official FIRST recording titled “Einstein 2 - 2022 FIRST Championship”; its visible description exactly matches red 1619/6672/254 scoring 164 and blue 3534/5940/6328 scoring 122. This establishes page identity, not independent visual identity. Keep that distinction if the video is mislabeled or contains a replay later in the file.

For each recording, preserve its exact URL, creator, available duration and any alternate-angle relation. Record whether a replay is the final scored attempt or an abandoned/no-score attempt. Do not silently overwrite the original evidence when substituting a better angle. In 2022 the semifinal stage is round-robin-style Einstein play; later double-elimination set/match keys use different conventions. Do not infer bracket order by sorting all seasons with the same filename heuristic.

## A continuous first pass plus six robot-follow passes

View the full match from prestart through the final action at a speed that preserves the interactions being asserted. Establish where autonomous starts, teleop starts and the match ends in the source video. Link every event to both source time and the visible match clock when available. For edited analysis with pauses, rewinds or slow motion, use a piecewise mapping rather than assuming source seconds equal elapsed match seconds. A caption timestamp is a navigation pointer until aligned visually.

Then follow each of the six robots through the full sequence. Record acquisition source, held inventory only when countable, scoring location and configuration, crossing choice, passing destination, screen/defense target and changes of job. For 2026, identify the actual hub state and the robot’s preparation for its next active window. For 2025, record concurrent L1, algae and branch work rather than imposing a serial “finish high branches, then do L1” story. For earlier seasons, preserve their own field geometry, scoring constraints and endgame incentives; do not import the 2026 supply model automatically.

A role is an interval, not a permanent label for a team or a robot. The same robot can score, pass, screen, steal, defend and recover in one match. A stopped robot can affect a route while providing no intended defensive action. A robot with a loaded hopper can influence supply without scoring. A defender may change targets to protect a crossing instead of following its original mark. Keep those possibilities distinguishable in the log.

## What an individual event needs

Store event ID, match key, recording ID, source start/end, match-clock start/end, actors, current configuration, field location, directly visible action, visible outcome, uncertainty and evidence links. Distinguish “robot contacts opponent,” “opponent changes route,” “shots fall short” and “robot stops moving.” Those observations do not by themselves mean “intentional pick,” “successful defense worth one hopper,” “battery sag” or “radio failure.” Put those interpretations in separate fields with their supporting or missing evidence.

For a screen or defensive handoff, observe all participants before and after the interaction. A five-second delay may save another defender’s travel, but it may also cost the screening scorer an equally valuable cycle. Track the alternative route actually available and the time remaining in the scoring window. Do not turn a rough hopper capacity into denied points. For a steal, distinguish fuel removed from an opponent’s reserve, fuel retained, fuel passed, fuel later scored and fuel lost back to the opponent. Avoid counting a transfer twice.

Leave unknown counts null. An empty event list means footage unreviewed, not that the match contained no relevant event. A camera cut creates a blind interval even if broadcast commentary continues. Multiple robots near a pile do not reveal their exact pickup share. Hub counts cannot generally assign individual scoring when streams overlap. Use the official score only at its actual alliance/phase resolution.

## Geometry and failures need more than a plausible story

Record the deployed envelope as seen at the interaction: extension can change a trench-capable robot into a bump-only robot. When a defender constrains rotation, identify the bumper contact and nearby hub, trench bar, wall or bump separately. Do not infer exact clearance, mass, traction, moment of inertia or motor current from a camera image. A rounded perimeter changes the contact problem but cannot guarantee escape under every friction and obstacle condition.

For an operational interruption, mark the last unambiguous functioning action, the first abnormal action, any recovery, and which capabilities remain. “Collects but shoots short” differs from “entire robot dead.” A mechanism appearing damaged is not a diagnosis of root cause. Electrical logs, operator testimony or a technical publication may explain a symptom later; preserve the chronology and attribution of that new explanation. Do not label an unobserved problem a brownout because the score dropped.

## Reconcile with official components without inventing individual output

Keep final score, clean score, penalties received and each relevant official phase or component. Reconcile arithmetic and identify which alliance had each active shift. Own first/second active-shift totals in 2026 occur at different wall-clock times for opponents. The final-period fuel component is not climb output. The stored 2026 finals all record zero tower points for both alliances; fuel and access remain the useful questions in this series.

For 2026 match 3, official auto fuel is 188–118; post-auto fuel is 529–509; final is 717–632 because Milstein receives five penalty points. The commentator’s post-auto numbers are alliance quantities. For match 6, clean output is 678–691 and final is 688–691, with ten penalty points received by Milstein. A three-point final is not a three-point clean result. Preserve this distinction in quizzes and causal explanations.

In the upper-bracket final, Daly wins auto 186–83 and transition 65–30 but does not win every subsequent fuel component. In finals 2 it does lead every recorded fuel component, with the final period only 169–165. In finals 3 the own active-shift totals are 311–79, while final-period fuel is 154–161. Those patterns guide what footage to investigate; they cannot identify how many fuel a defender individually denied.

## Completion and verification

Do not set complete=true until full interval coverage, all-six-robot follow checks, identity and clock alignment, camera blind spots, score reconciliation and explicit unresolved claims are present. It is acceptable for a completed viewing to leave a particular action unresolved because it is occluded. That uncertainty must remain visible; viewing completion is not omniscience. A user correction should identify the event/claim, the better source or timestamp, the revised interpretation and which downstream design conclusions need reconsideration.

The intended next step is playable match footage or an authorized usable video source. Until it exists, the six expanded 2026 narratives remain commentary evidence, and all eighty visual records remain pending. The JSONL ledger is the durable queue; it is not a certification of work that could not be performed.

title: 2022-604 primary-source mechanisms and strategic context
body:
# 2022-604 — Quixilver: Octopus Prime

Primary source: https://github.com/frc604/2022-public

Reviewed 2026-10-26. This is a source-bounded technical study. Construction, stated intent, interpretation and unresolved evidence are separate.

Code commit: 2cfd645d19ac09681d201481e8eecd10156b2b9d. Read the original FRC-2022 tree. FRC-2022-NEW is a learning rewrite, not certified event code. File locators: Intake.java, BallPath.java, Launcher.java, Climber.java and Calibration.java under FRC-2022/src/com/_604robotics/robot2022/.

## Published FRC-2022 code · drivetrain

### Published construction or code

Calibration defines a 20.5-inch wheelbase and track width, 3.94-inch wheel diameter, 6.75:1 drive reduction and 12.8:1 steering reduction. These are software configuration values, not independent measurements.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Mechanical selection rationale is not established by the code.

### Engineering interpretation

The swerve and localization must be considered together. A configured maximum speed is not a demonstrated match speed. Wheel calibration affects both the path tracker and the launch-distance estimate, so a copied drive configuration can corrupt scoring even when teleop feels acceptable. Check hardware revision, encoder scales and actual loaded wheel circumference before borrowing constants.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Published FRC-2022 code · intake

### Published construction or code

Intake.java configures distinct Falcon 500 roller and deployment motors, a trapezoidal deployment profile, arm feedforward and a 45A deployment stator limit. Intake, eject, unjam and yeet commands are separate entry points.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The code does not state why this exact mechanical geometry was selected.

### Engineering interpretation

The published interface treats recovery and reverse flow as designed operating modes. That is useful architectural evidence, but it does not establish roller material, width, compression or impact survival. A profiled pivot can reduce abrupt actuation; whether it does so under contact depends on the real mechanism and controller settings. Preserve these unknowns rather than infer a later 604 polycarbonate intake in 2022.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Published FRC-2022 code · transfer

### Published construction or code

BallPath.java separates upper and lower Falcon-driven transport sections and exposes position/velocity control and sensor-based ball handling.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Exact transport geometry and team selection rationale remain unresolved.

### Engineering interpretation

Separately controlled transport can stage a second cargo while releasing the first, but introduces coordination between occupancy sensing, launcher readiness and reverse recovery. Code supports the existence of these interfaces, not an independent throughput result or proof of jam-free behavior. A two-cargo game rewards preserving a reliable staged sequence; extra transport complexity should be justified by actual scoring continuity.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Published FRC-2022 code · scoring

### Published construction or code

Launcher.java configures front and rear Falcon flywheel motors with feedforward and feedback. Readiness checks use a five-sample speed buffer and tolerance; distance-related bounds are treated separately.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The source establishes readiness logic, not a published mechanical reason for wheel geometry.

### Engineering interpretation

Requiring recent samples within tolerance is different from checking one instantaneous RPM. It can reject a momentary speed crossing after spin-up or a previous shot. The trade is delayed release versus launch consistency. The existence of front/rear motors does not establish independent spin control in competition, wheel dimensions, a turret, or exact release angle. Those require geometry and event evidence.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Published FRC-2022 code · endgame

### Published construction or code

Climber.java configures three NEO motors and staged first-rung, lift, handoff, high-rung and traversal transitions. It uses filtered tilt and tilt rate, position/profile completion and an angle-history lockout.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Comments explicitly describe gyro-controlled transitions and an antenna-touch-angle lockout; broader hardware intent is not fully documented here.

### Engineering interpretation

This is a dynamic climb sequence, not a simple winch toggle. A transition may require both operator approval and a suitable swing/position state. That ties compliance, sensor filtering, angular thresholds and operator timing together. A traversal state in released code proves intended capability, not a successful traversal in every match or that all events ran this revision. Exact hook and support geometry remain open.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Original code versus learning rewrite · controls

### Published construction or code

The repository README identifies FRC-2022 as robot code and FRC-2022-NEW as a work-in-progress reimplementation for learning and cleanup. Quikplan-swerve and the offboard quixpf particle filter are separate directories.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The rewrite is explicitly described as preparation and learning.

### Engineering interpretation

Do not read the cleaner NEW tree and retroactively claim every behavior was fielded in 2022. The original tree is the stronger starting point for event-era behavior, though its final commit still lacks per-event installation certification. Pin the repository commit and file path when citing code; preserve the distinction between software configuration, mechanical construction and observed performance.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Evidence limits

- Selected primary publications/code reviewed; exact per-event installation and exhaustive intermediate revisions remain unresolved.
- Four previously blocked source originals (2023 robot photo; 2026 serializer, intake and hopper CAD views) were recovered through normal browser downloads on 2026-10-26 and inspected. Whole-robot source views are not exhaustive mechanism or event-version certification.

# 2023-604 — Quixilver: 2023 published robot (name not independently confirmed)

Primary source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-604-quixilver-presents-our-2023-robot-and-code-release/447255

Reviewed 2026-10-26. This is a source-bounded technical study. Construction, stated intent, interpretation and unresolved evidence are separate.

## 2023 published robot account · intake

### Published construction or code

A pasta-roller intake grips a cone flange and pinches a cube, constraining cones to tip-in or tip-out. A roller reorienter supplies the additional rotational degree of freedom needed for an upright handoff. Rollers are powered coaxially through the reorienter.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The team wanted ground pickup in arbitrary orientations; human-player throwing could shorten travel by an estimated 40% and reduce loading-zone traffic. Coaxial drive protects motors and reduces mass at the intake edge.

### Engineering interpretation

This is an explicit strategy-to-mechanism chain: changing the pickup source reduces travel only if orientation and handoff remain reliable. The 40% is the team’s route estimate, not an independently measured cycle improvement. A broad capture envelope transfers complexity downstream unless the robot can reduce the resulting pose uncertainty. Compare full acquisition-to-scoring cycles, including difficult orientations, rather than pickup speed alone.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## 2023 published robot account · transfer

### Published construction or code

A linear intake slider brings the piece inward and permits frontal compliance. A separate horizontal scoring-arm slider reaches across the intake. A time-of-flight sensor first distinguishes orientation at a fixed location, then locates the piece laterally. The elevator lowers while the intake expels to hand off.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The team needed handoff despite variable piece position across the intake width.

### Engineering interpretation

Do not collapse the two sliders into a single motion. The intake reduces some uncertainty, then sensing and the receiving mechanism handle what remains. This avoids requiring perfect passive centering, at the cost of coordinated motion, sensor interpretation and collision clearance. Sensor occlusion, flange shape, cone reflectivity and loaded mechanism deflection are plausible validation concerns, not failures established by this publication.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## 2023 published robot account · scoring

### Published construction or code

A non-parallel four-bar provides scoring reach. An Everybot-style lightweight gripper squeezes the cone tip and pinches a cube. The release describes scoring all levels.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The team chose the linkage for low mass and long extension, and judged the high-versus-middle scoring difference sufficient to justify the added capability.

### Engineering interpretation

The linkage choice belongs with the piece acquisition and handoff design. Saving moving mass can reduce the drive and tipping burden, but linkage workspace, joint play and gripper compliance determine the usable placement envelope. A later team using a single-stage elevator should not be read as proof that this four-bar was a failed architecture; the game, interface and required motion differ.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## 2023 published robot account · controls

### Published construction or code

Originally the operator selected scoring locations on a driverstation keyboard and the driver triggered automated scoring. The team later reports the driver becoming faster and more consistent than that sequence, reducing the operator role to piece and level selection.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The control allocation evolved with driver performance.

### Engineering interpretation

Automation should be judged against practiced human operation, including recovery, rather than valued simply because it exists. This is a useful counterexample to treating 604’s later single-driver automation as an unchanging philosophy implemented identically every year. Keep the final software release and its 2024-beta port distinct. Detailed drivetrain specifications and the charge-station balancing mechanism are not established by this reviewed release.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Evidence limits

- Selected primary publications/code reviewed; exact per-event installation and exhaustive intermediate revisions remain unresolved.
- Four previously blocked source originals (2023 robot photo; 2026 serializer, intake and hopper CAD views) were recovered through normal browser downloads on 2026-10-26 and inspected. Whole-robot source views are not exhaustive mechanism or event-version certification.

The reviewed publication does not establish charge-station balance construction or exact drivetrain hardware. FIRST’s carried-forward robot-name field is not treated as authoritative identity for this different-season machine.


## Recovered original source images · 2026-10-26

The earlier direct-download failures are resolved. These are unchanged originals from the team release; the labels below are editorial retrieval aids. Inspect the full view before borrowing packaging ideas. Exact dimensions, hidden construction and match performance require independent source evidence.

# 2024-604 — Quixilver: Domotron

Primary source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-604-quixilver-presents-our-2024-robot-cad-and-code-release/477799

Reviewed 2026-10-26. This is a source-bounded technical study. Construction, stated intent, interpretation and unresolved evidence are separate.

## 2024 release and May 2025 follow-up · intake

### Published construction or code

Polycarbonate rollers flex under impact; short dead-axle sections avoid a full-width shaft permanently bending. The team reports rollers deflecting more than half their diameter in bad hits. Deployment ties the two sides through chain and a cross shaft inside the frame.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Compliance, weight and packaging drove the split-axle construction. The team explicitly reports axle-mount bolts shearing and deployment chain snapping, unresolved during the season.

### Engineering interpretation

A compliant roller is not the same as a robust entire intake. Moving deformation away from a long shaft can concentrate load in axle bolts or a mechanically coupled deployment system. This matters directly to 1833’s request for something beefy: copy the load path and its known limitations, not merely the visible material. The 2026 independently driven arms are a later response to the chain failure, not a configuration that existed throughout 2024.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## 2024 published CAD versus installed hardware · controls

### Published construction or code

The team says bellypan holes were hand-drilled and omitted from CAD, electronics were suppressed to reduce CAD lag, shooter shafts were actually cut shorter, and a reused climber shaft tensioned surgical tubing absent from CAD.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Some differences were drafting omissions, some deliberate reuse and some effort-versus-benefit decisions.

### Engineering interpretation

A released CAD assembly is a valuable geometry reference but not a perfect as-built record. A long shaft in a rendering is not automatically an intended design feature. Likewise, suppressed electronics do not imply an unplanned electrical layout. Follow the team’s replies when interpreting the release. The existing interview synopsis documents the asymmetric launcher and trap system; this addition focuses on the explicitly published manufacturing and intake corrections.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

- Only source-established configurations and changes are described; intermediate revisions may remain unresolved.
